children: OTTAWA--Canadian manufactured goods prices continued to march higher last month as the resumption of the conflict between the U.S. and Iran drove up energy prices.
Statistics Canada's industrial product price index increased 1.3% in July from the month before. Compared with a year earlier, prices were 13.5% higher, a 23rd straight annual increase.

The monthly advance was sharper than the 0.8% rise in the index expected by economists, and follows a softer 0.3% increase in producer prices in June. The continued increase in prices hints at inflation risk for Canadians at a time when the central bank is wary of the spike in energy costs this year passing through more broadly into higher prices.
Prices for raw materials bought by manufacturers operating in the country also increased between July and August, and showed another jump from last year.

Bank of Canada officials expect consumer inflation to remain elevated in the near term given persistently high gasoline prices as the conflict in the Middle East drags on. They also have warned of a likely hit to business and consumer confidence as fresh U.S. tariffs on Canadian exports possibly hampers economic activity, which had rebounded strongly in the second quarter of the year.
Consumer price inflation held steady in August at the top end of the 1%-to-3% window the Bank of Canada aims for, as gasoline prices rose less sharply but travel costs and rents increased.

The monthly rise in the industrial product price index for August was driven by energy and petroleum products, including a jump in diesel fuel and in light fuel oils. Excluding energy and petroleum, producer prices were up 0.8% from the month before after falling 0.6% in July, the national data agency said.

Prices for non-ferrous metal products also increased during the month, after consecutive declines in June and July, as unwrought gold, silver and platinum group metals rose for the first time since January. Chemicals prices also were higher in August after weakness the month before that reversed some of the sharp gains earlier in the year.

The industrial product price index measures the prices that manufacturers in Canada receive once their goods leave the plant. It doesn't reflect the final prices consumers pay for goods on store shelves.
Prices for raw materials, which track costs paid by manufacturers, were up 3.1% in August and 22.8% higher than a year ago after an 18.2% annual rise a month prior.

Crude energy products were the main driver of the monthly increase, followed by metal ores, concentrates and scrap. The increase was moderated slightly by lower prices for animals and animal products.
Excluding crude energy products, raw material prices were up 1.1% from July and 17.2% compared with a year earlier.
